Define Observation Points

Assume that nine thermometers are positioned at specific locations as shown below. These thermometers provide observed temperature data, which will be used to infer the unknown boundary condition in the 2D heat transfer problem.


The cell selects the grid indices $15$, $50$ and $85$ in each direction and takes all nine combinations, giving a regular $3\times3$ array of sensors at coordinates approximately $-0.697$, $0.010$ and $0.717$ in each axis. They therefore sit well inside the domain, none of them close to the unknown top edge, which is realistic: an inaccessible boundary is inaccessible to instrumentation as well.


Nine numbers is a thin diet even compared with the seventeen of Section 4, and the unknown here is not a pair of scalars but an entire function along an edge. That mismatch is why Section 5.3 improves the answer without perfecting it, and why Section 5.4 needs to supply structure rather than more data.


The plot shows the finite difference field with the nine sensor locations marked in red. Read the field before continuing: the right edge is hot at $T=1$, the left edge is at $T=0.5$, the bottom edge is cold at $T=0$, and the top edge is where the interesting question lies.

Define Collocation Points

A $100\times100$ lattice gives ten thousand interior collocation points, and each of the four edges is sampled with a hundred points; the last lines turn every point set into a tensor on the selected device, with gradients tracked only for the interior points, where the equation is differentiated. Note that the top edge is included in the point sets even though no condition is imposed on it in this section; it will be needed in Section 5.4, where the prior knowledge term is evaluated there, and in Section 5.5, where the recovered profile is plotted along it.

Define PINN Network

Two inputs, one output, four hidden layers of two hundred and fifty-six units, with Adam at a learning rate of $10^{-4}$. The network is nearly as large as the Navier-Stokes network of Section 4, which is generous for a linear equation in a single field. Since the whole section is a comparison between three training regimes, a fixed and generous architecture is the right choice: it removes capacity from the list of possible explanations for the differences observed.


The plotting helper draws the reference field, the current prediction, and the absolute error, with the error panel's colour scale fixed to $[0, 0.2]$ so that the three regimes can be compared on identical terms. Fixing that scale by hand is what makes the comparison in Sections 8.3 and 8.4 legible.


In [32]:
class PINN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(PINN, self).__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2, 256),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(256, 256),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(256, 256),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(256, 256),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(256, 1)
        )
        for m in self.net:
            if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
                nn.init.xavier_normal_(m.weight)
                nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)

model = PINN().to(device)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr = 1e-4)

Define Functions to Compute Physics Loss

The same helper as before.


In [34]:
def derivative(y, t):
    df = torch.autograd.grad(y, t, grad_outputs = torch.ones_like(y), create_graph = True)[0]
    df_x = df[:, 0:1]
    df_y = df[:, 1:2]
    return df_x, df_y

Define Governing Equation and Three Known Boundary Conditions

The residual function takes two derivatives in each direction and returns $\kappa(T_{xx} + T_{yy})$ with $\kappa = 1$ written explicitly as a factor. The three boundary functions evaluate the network on the bottom, right and left edges and subtract the prescribed values $0$, $1$ and $0.5$ respectively.


There is no function for the top edge. That absence is the entire content of this section, and it is worth pausing on the fact that nothing in the code will complain about it. The loss will be assembled from four terms, will descend, and will produce a field. The missing physics announces itself nowhere except in the answer.


In [35]:
def PDE(model, Y_domain):
    T = model(Y_domain)

    dT_x, dT_y = derivative(T, Y_domain)
    dT_xx, _ = derivative(dT_x, Y_domain)
    _, dT_yy = derivative(dT_y, Y_domain)

    pde = 1 * (dT_xx + dT_yy)
    return pde

def BC_bottom(model, Y_bottom):
    T_bottom = model(Y_bottom)
    return T_bottom

def BC_right(model, Y_right):
    T_right = model(Y_right)
    return T_right - 1

def BC_left(model, Y_left):
    T_left = model(Y_left)
    return T_left - 0.5

Train

Twenty thousand epochs with


$$ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{PDE}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{bottom}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{right}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{left}}, $$


and no term for the top edge and no data. This is the pure physics baseline, and the diagnostic figure is redrawn every thousand epochs so that the field can be watched as it forms.

Result

As shown, the prediction deviates significantly from the ground truth due to the absence of one boundary condition, and the reason is the absent condition rather than any failure of training. It is worth being precise about the two contrasting behaviours.


Most conventional computational methods cannot produce any result at all unless every boundary condition is specified, because a missing condition leaves their system of equations singular or under-determined and the solve fails outright. A PINN never assembles such a system. It minimizes a penalty, and a penalty that says nothing about the top edge simply leaves the network free there; the optimizer settles on whichever admissible field its initialization and its trajectory happen to lead it to.


This is directly analogous to an under-determined system of linear equations, which has infinitely many solutions and whose standard algorithms return one particular member of the family, typically the one of smallest norm, without any indication that others exist. A PINN behaves the same way and offers the same false comfort: the loss will look small, because the terms in it really are being satisfied, and the answer will still be wrong.

5.3. Lab 2: Inverse Problem with Observed Data¶

We now incorporate the readings from the nine sensors, giving the PINN more information with which to infer the missing boundary condition.


The analogy with systems of equations carries over exactly. Adding nine observations adds nine conditions on the same unknowns, pushing the problem from under-determined towards over-determined, and an over-determined system is handled by least squares, returning the solution that best satisfies all constraints simultaneously. That is precisely what minimizing a sum of squared residuals does, and it is why the sum-of-squares form of the PINN loss is the right one rather than merely a convenient one.


Nine numbers cannot determine an entire boundary profile, so we should expect improvement rather than resolution. The interesting question, which Section 5.5 answers, is how much of the profile nine interior temperatures can recover.


Train with data

The model is rebuilt from scratch so that the comparison is clean, then trained for the same twenty thousand epochs with the identical optimizer and learning rate. The loss now carries one additional term,


$$ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{PDE}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{BC}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{data}}, $$


with $\mathcal{L}_{\text{data}}$ the mean squared error between the network's prediction and the nine measured temperatures. Its weight is $1$, in contrast to the $10$ used in Section 4. The difference in circumstances justifies the difference in weight: there the data term was the sole means of identifying two scalars against nineteen thousand collocation points, while here it competes against a merely under-determined physics loss and is not being asked to fix a scale.

5.4. Lab 3: Inverse Problem with Observed Data and Prior Knowledge¶

To make this example more interesting, let us assume that we have prior knowledge that the temperature at the missing boundary is unknown but constant. This is a very ordinary kind of engineering knowledge. An edge in contact with a large well-stirred reservoir, or with a boiling liquid, or with a block of high-conductivity metal, is at a uniform temperature whether or not anyone has measured it.


The information is qualitative, and it is not a boundary condition in the usual sense, since it names no value. It is nevertheless enormously informative. The space of possible top-edge profiles collapses from an infinite-dimensional function space to a single real number, and nine sensors are ample to determine one number.


Expressing "constant but unknown" as a loss

The implementation is three lines and is the most elegant construction in this notebook. Evaluate the network along the top edge to get $T_{\text{top}}$, compute the mean of those values, and penalize the mean squared deviation of the values from their own mean:


$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{prior}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(T_\theta(x_i, 1) - \bar{T}\right)^2, \qquad \bar{T} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} T_\theta(x_j, 1). $$


This is exactly the sample variance of the predicted top-edge temperature. It is zero when and only when the profile is constant, and it says nothing whatever about which constant. The target of the mean squared error is not a fixed number supplied by the modeller but a quantity computed from the network's own output, and because it is computed with ordinary differentiable operations, gradients flow through it: the penalty pushes each edge value towards the current mean while the mean itself is free to drift to wherever the rest of the loss wants it.


The general lesson is worth extracting from the special case. Anything you know about the solution that can be written as a differentiable function of the network output, vanishing when the knowledge is respected, can be added to the loss as a term. Monotonicity, symmetry, non-negativity, a bound, an integral constraint, a known asymptotic slope: these are all expressible in the same way. The PINN loss is not restricted to differential equations. It is a place to put everything you know, which is the theme Embedding Prior Knowledge into Neural Networks develops at length.


Train again using both data and prior knowledge

The model is rebuilt once more and trained for the same twenty thousand epochs with


$$ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{PDE}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{BC}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{data}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{prior}}, $$


all weights equal to one. Predict the outcome before running it. The physics fixes the field given the boundary, the prior reduces the unknown boundary to a single number, and nine sensors overdetermine that number comfortably. This model should be much better than the previous two, and it should be better mostly near the top edge, where the previous models had nothing to go on.

Result

It is clearly observed that the final prediction is the most accurate among the three different scenarios, which was predictable from an information argument alone and did not require running anything. Two conclusions follow.


The first concerns the PINN framework itself. We have now seen it absorb three different kinds of knowledge into a single objective function: a governing equation, a set of measurements, and a qualitative structural fact. All three entered in the same way, as a non-negative term that vanishes when the knowledge is respected, and all three were minimized by the same optimizer in the same loop. That uniformity is the framework's real strength, more than any individual result in this notebook.


The second is a strategy for engineering problems generally. When addressing a complex engineering challenge, begin by asking what data is available, and then, rather than stopping there, ask what else is known: governing equations, boundary conditions, conservation laws, symmetries, monotonicity, bounds, results from a simplified analysis, or the engineer's judgement that a certain surface must be at uniform temperature. Each such item is a constraint, each constraint is a term, and each term reduces the size of the space in which the answer is being sought. Data is one source of information among several, and in engineering it is frequently the scarcest.



5.5. What the Three Labs Showed¶

To evaluate the models' performance more precisely, we plot the predicted temperature along the top boundary itself. This gives a direct comparison against the ground truth and shows how well each model captured the missing boundary condition.


This is the right diagnostic and the reason is worth stating. The colour maps of the interior compare fields that are dominated by the three known edges, so all three models look broadly similar in them; the disagreement is concentrated at the top, where a small region of a colour map conveys very little. Plotting the recovered profile along the unknown edge isolates the quantity that was actually being inferred and puts all three models on one set of axes against the ground truth.


The ground truth appears in the plot as a line of zeros: the true temperature along the top edge is uniformly zero. Note that this is consistent with the prior knowledge used in Section 5.4, which asserted uniformity without naming the value, and that the value itself was never supplied to any of the three models.


Predict the three curves before looking. The model without data has no information about the edge at all, so its profile can be anything and should be furthest from zero. The model with data has nine interior constraints and should be closer but uneven along the edge, since nothing forces it to be flat. The model with the prior should be nearly flat by construction, at whichever constant the sensors imply.


In [44]:
model_wo_data = torch.load('/content/lab4_wo_data.pt', map_location = device, weights_only = False)
model_w_data = torch.load('/content/lab4_w_data.pt', map_location = device, weights_only = False)
model_w_prior = torch.load('/content/lab4_w_prior.pt', map_location = device, weights_only = False)

x_top = Y_top[:, 0].cpu().numpy()

T_wo_data = model_wo_data(Y_top).detach().cpu().numpy().flatten()
T_w_data = model_w_data(Y_top).detach().cpu().numpy().flatten()
T_w_prior = model_w_prior(Y_top).detach().cpu().numpy().flatten()

plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.plot(x_top, np.zeros_like(x_top), c = 'k', linestyle = '--', linewidth = 2, label = 'GT')
plt.plot(x_top, T_wo_data, c = 'b', linestyle = '--', linewidth = 2, label = 'w/o data')
plt.plot(x_top, T_w_data, c = 'g', linestyle = '--', linewidth = 2, label = 'w/ data')
plt.plot(x_top, T_w_prior, c = 'r', linewidth = 2, label = 'w/ prior')
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('Temperature, T')
plt.title('Predicted Temperature along the Top Boundary')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

The plot confirms the ordering, and the shapes of the curves are as informative as their distances from the truth. The unconstrained model wanders; the data-only model is pulled towards the truth in the middle of the edge, where the sensors have most influence, and drifts near the corners where they have least; the model with the prior is flat, because flatness is what the variance penalty enforces, and sits close to zero, because that is where nine interior temperatures place the constant.


One last observation to close the section. The improvement from the second model to the third came from no new measurements whatsoever. It came from writing down something the engineer already knew. That is a good note on which to leave inverse problems.





Summary¶


Key takeaways

  • The same four-part recipe solved a fourth-order boundary value problem in solid mechanics, a first-order nonlinear initial value problem in fluid mechanics, and a coupled three-state system in epidemiology. Between them, only the residual function changed.
  • The forward problem is not where a PINN earns its place. On all three problems it competes with numerical methods that are faster and more accurate. The inverse problem is different: the unknown property is one more trainable number in the same loss, and nothing else about the method has to change to accommodate it.
  • Physics alone may not identify a parameter. In the beam, any $E$ satisfies the equation and all four boundary conditions if the displacement is rescaled by $1/E$; in the tank, the residual is equally content with a family of values of $C$. In both cases the loss is small and the answer is wrong — a failure that no amount of further training reveals.
  • A few observations close the system, because they fix the scale that the physics leaves free. Nine readings sufficed for the beam and for the tank, and twenty noisy observations of the infected fraction alone recovered both $\beta$ and $\gamma$ in the SIR model.
  • Where the observations are placed matters. The sensitivity $\partial h/\partial C$ vanishes at both ends of the drainage problem, so a sensor there would carry no information about $C$; the readings belong in the middle. The same argument puts the beam's sensors away from the supports, where the displacement is pinned to zero whatever the stiffness.
  • Scales are balanced by hand. The beam's displacements are small enough that the data term needs a factor of $1000$ before it can compete with the residual, and the SIR loss weights the data and the initial conditions by $10$. These weights are chosen, not derived, and they are the most fragile part of a PINN.
  • The unknown does not have to be a scalar. In the heated plate it is a function along an edge, which nine interior readings can improve but not resolve. What resolves it is a piece of qualitative knowledge, that the edge is at a uniform temperature, written as the variance of the network's own prediction along that edge — a penalty that names no value and collapses an infinite-dimensional unknown to one number.
  • Two properties can be identified at once, and in a non-linear system: the density and the viscosity of the flow past a cylinder are recovered to about one percent from seventeen velocity readings, the viscosity travelling two orders of magnitude from its initial guess. The estimates are trustworthy because their traces flatten, not because the final numbers look plausible.
  • Two small devices recur: learn $\log\theta$ when $\theta$ must stay positive, and add a conservation term such as $\hat S + \hat I + \hat R = 1$ when the system has an invariant that the equations only imply.

Looking ahead. Every loss in this notebook was a sum of terms whose weights were chosen by hand, and the results depended on those choices. How to set them — and how to avoid having to set them at all — is the subject of Regularization, MAP Estimation, and Loss Weighting.
